subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER  INFORMATION RESPECTING NATO NOT GIVEN TO PARLIAMENT

speechtext:
Right Hon, J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question affecting the privileges of this House of Commons. The NATO council meeting has continued for a couple of days. Parliament has not received any information whatever regarding the stand taken by Canada, yet the press from day to day contains statements. Last night's Canadian Press sets out the following:
The way has been cleared for the creation of an Atlantic alliance with nuclear strike forces with Canada one of the contributing countries. Today NATO foreign ministers switched their attention to world trouble spots. General agreement on the basic idea of the type of force to be built initially around Polaris-firing submarines and British long range bombers was reached.
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the press is regularly given information by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the minister of defence. This information is not made available to parliament. I will say no more at this time except that this constitutes a derogation from the rights of parliament. Controlled news is something which should not exist in this parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was asked yesterday if I would give a report on the discussions that took place in London and Geneva in connection with the general agreement on tariffs and trade. I should now like to do so.
As hon. members are aware, the meeting of the economic consultative committee took place in London on May 13 and 14 just before the meeting of trade ministers held in Geneva under the auspices of the general agreement on tariffs and trade from May 16 to 21. I beg leave first to table copies of the communique issued at the conclusion of the commonwealth meeting, and of the resolutions and other conclusions adopted by the trade ministers in Geneva.
28902-5-16J

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext: Is it agreed that the minister have leave to table these documents?

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext:
At the London meetings, Mr. Speaker, I was impressed by the variety of the modern commonwealth. It seems to me that this is a reflection of the modern world, the free world at least. The whole spectrum of needs and aspirations is represented in the commonwealth. We have Britain, a highly industrialized country, Canada and Australia which are major exporters of agricultural and primary products as well as manufacturers of more limited scale, and New Zealand almost entirely dependant on agriculture. I was impressed with the fact that the modern commonwealth includes a majority now of newly independent countries only recently embarked on the process of development and diversification.
It was a rewarding experience for me to meet the trade ministers of these commonwealth countries, the new as well as the old. In London we were able to discuss in the unique and understanding atmosphere of commonwealth meetings that is familiar to so many of us the interests and approaches of the different members to the major current issues of trade and development.
Three main questions were on the agenda. First, the expansion of the trade of the developing countries; second, world trade in agricultural products, and third the proposal for a further major round of negotiations to reduce tariffs and other barriers to world trade. At the meeting there was also an opportunity to review the situation in Europe and to hear from the British ministers about developments since the termination of the Brussels talks.
All the ministers recognized the continuing significance of commonwealth trade. We were also agreed on the need for a general expansion of world trade and on the importance of this for all commonwealth countries.
As hon. members will see from the text of the communique which I have just tabled, the needs of the less advanced countries of the commonwealth received full recognition, and Canada joined with other members of the commonwealth in promising our support for action to help meet these needs, both at the subsequent GATT ministerial meeting

Report on GATT Conference and at the forthcoming United Nations conference on trade and development, the preparatory committee for which is now meeting in Geneva.
At the GATT meeting in Geneva the purpose was to come to grips on a world wide basis with the three major trade problems discussed in London. These problems are difficult and complex, and many conflicting interests remain to be resolved in the long negotiations that lie ahead. Nevertheless the countries concerned have agreed to come to the negotiating table and a start will be made. This was a tremendous and heartening achievement.
For the developing countries decisions were taken to facilitate expansion of their trade, and machinery had been established to keep their problems in the forefront of the negotiations and of GATT discussions. But on many points views differed as to the best way to proceed, notably between the European economic community and the overseas countries associated with the community on the one hand, and the developing nations in the commonwealth and elsewhere in the world on the other.
These differences are reflected in the documents I have tabled. But there was no disagreement on the urgency and fundamental importance of moving to help all these countries to meet the challenges of their development and the fundamental need to improve the lot of their peoples. Aid is clearly not enough. Financial and technical assistance must be accompanied by better opportunities to trade and other measures to facilitate the expansion and stability of the export earnings of these countries.
The Geneva conference of GATT was the fifth meeting of GATT ministers since the general agreement was signed in 1947, and the chief purpose of this meeting was to initiate a major negotiation for the reduction of tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade. The new United States authority to cut the protection surrounding the United States market made these negotiations possible. The power contained in the trade expansion act to reduce most United States tariffs by half and to remove duties that are 5 per cent or less is both imaginative and far reaching. It provides more scope to reduce American protection than has been available for many, many years.
The proposal for new and substantial negotiations, the so called Kennedy round, was strongly supported by Canada, by Britain and by many other countries whose interest lies in the expansion of world trade. The meeting agreed that negotiations should be

joined and that they should cover trade barriers of all kinds and all sectors of trade.
Agreement was also reached that the negotiation plan should be based on the principle of equal across the board tariff reduction subject to certain exceptions and subject to the working out of procedures to narrow differences in tariff levels between major industrial powers where these have significant effects on trade.
As hon. members will be aware from the newspaper reports that came back from Geneva, many days of negotiations between the United States and the European economic community were necessary before the final formula affecting the principle of negotiation was agreed upon.
I made it clear that for Canada such a formula of tariff reduction would not yield the necessary mutuality of trade and economic benefit. I indicated that for a country like Canada, with its limited domestic market, its patterns of production and trade and its relatively narrow range of exports, it would be difficult to find any single formula that would achieve the necessary balance of advantage. I assured the meeting, however, that Canada would play its part and make concessions in Canadian tariffs commensurate with the benefits we receive.
The conclusions of the meeting cover the position of Canada and certain other countries in a somewhat similar position. I should like to quote these provisions so that members of the house will understand how the negotiations concluded. The conclusions provide that the tariff negotiations committee which was established at our meeting shall deal with, inter alia, and I quote:
The problem for certain countries with a very low average level of tariffs or with a special economic or trade structure such that equal linear tariff reductions may not provide an adequate balance of advantages.
In his statement which forms an integral part of the conclusions of the meeting the chairman of the GATT ministerial meeting stated that pursuant to this paragraph, and I quote:
The committee will deal with the case of certain countries where it is established that their very low average level of tariffs or their economic or trade structure is such that the general application of equal linear tariff reductions would not be appropriate. For such countries the objective shall be the negotiation of a balance of advantages based on trade concessions by them of equivalent value, not excluding equal linear reductions where appropriate.
In addition, the chairman was asked during the concluding meeting whether the words "special economic or trade structure" in the resolution covered the special situation of a country which, it is established, has a very

large dependence on exports of agricultural and other primary products, and the chairman replied that this was the case.
I am satisfied that the United States and our other major trade partners fully understand Canada's position.
World trade in agricultural products presents particularly difficult problems. The normal trade rules have not been applied here, and efficient agricultural exporters like Canada have faced much frustration. It is significant therefore that agreement was reached in Geneva, including agreement by the European economic community, that agriculture shall be included in the negotiations. There is no doubt a settlement will be difficult to find, but with so much at stake, particularly with respect to wheat and other cereals, I can assure hon. members that the representatives of Canada at the forthcoming discussion will make every effort to ensure that these negotiations succeed. There are to be early meetings to discuss cereals and meats and a special group has been set up for dairy products.
These discussions may lead to new or revised international commodity arrangements.
In this connection, I would draw the attention of the house to the statement made Wednesday of this week in the British House of Commons by Mr. Christopher Soames, the minister of agriculture. I should also draw the attention of hon. members to the speech made by Lord Amory, which is on the same subject, reported in the Globe and Mail this morning. Mr. Soames forecast important changes in British agricultural support and import policies, and indicated British willingness to participate in further negotiations of international arrangements for temperate foodstuffs. I had the opportunity to discuss these matters with Mr. Soames, and we look forward to working closely with Britain, other importers and our fellow exporters of cereals and other products in the negotiations which are scheduled to open immediately.
Agreement at Geneva on the major points that I have mentioned was by no means easy. Much remains to be done and many difficulties overcome before there can be confidence that the various negotiations will yield a substantial and positive result. The stage has, however, been set for further progress if there is real willingness to make the negotiations a success. We propose, and I am now speaking in the name of Canada, to play a full and active part.
A busy timetable for negotiations has been agreed. In addition to the agricultural groups
Report on GATT Conference I have mentioned, a tariff negotiations committee will meet with a first task of working out the detailed negotiating rules by August
1.	These preparations are to lead up to a major trade conference opening on May 4 of next year, which will bring together the various elements and carry the negotiations forward toward completion. In preparation for the negotiations the government will wish to consult fully with all Canadian interests which may be affected. Procedures to this end will be announced in due course.
As one of the world's leading trading nations, whose economic well-being heavily depends on trade, Canada has much to gain from the success of the negotiations and the new export opportunities that will be opened up. This is true for our manufacturing as for our agricultural and primary production. Lower trade barriers can contribute in an important way to the efficient development of Canadian industry on the basis of wider markets. Successful negotiations will provide the opportunity to develop an improved pattern of production and trade which would give a stimulus to Canadian growth and employment on a suitable and competitive basis and so contribute to the development of Canada and the prosperity of the Canadian people.

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with a great deal of interest to this report of the two meetings, one in London and one in Geneva, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has just read to us. I think in some reports on international gatherings there is a tendency to exaggerate the results accomplished and to gloss over or minimize the difficulties which still remain to be resolved. As the minister has said, there are many difficulties in this area which have hardly been touched upon. I think, judging from press reports-and they were unanimous in this respect-that the conference at Geneva nearly broke down. It was not until the last day, and almost the last hour of the last day, that some agreement or some compromise was worked out which permitted the conference to adjourn, while officials carried on in attempting to establish some ground rules.
As I see it, that is about what was done. An agreement is to be reached on the ground rules under which future negotiations could be conducted. Apparently at the moment the officials will be engaged in trying to establish ground rules which would permit future negotiations.
The minister spoke about the complexity of the changing commonwealth which he

Report on GATT Conference found at London. I am sure that is a situation which everyone realizes, the complexity of the commonwealth and its rapidly changing basis, which perhaps explains why it is much more difficult to accomplish concrete objectives in that area when one is faced with this complexity than it is when one is on the outside and can airily suggest the ease with which these things could be accomplished.
In the press which, of course, I have seen this morning, it is reported that three of the commonwealth countries almost refused to concur in this tentative agreement, and with some reluctance they were persuaded to accept it. This is a report from the Wall Street Journal, not necessarily always an authentic and objective source of information, but it is fairly reliable. If it is correct I suppose the commonwealth countries referred to were Australia, New Zealand and Canada, and one must wonder what arguments were finally used to persuade them to accept.
Mr. MacEwan, the deputy premier of Australia, is quoted in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of yesterday's date by Mr. Eric Dennis, who was in Geneva, as saying that this marked the death knell of the British commonwealth preferential system. If that report is correct-and everyone knows it has been United States policy for many years to bring about the destruction of the preferential system-it is certainly going to add to the problems of agriculture to which my hon. friend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) referred yesterday. It will not only add to the problems of marketing wheat but also to apples, in which I have more than an academic interest at the moment.
In so far as Geneva is concerned, as the minister has said, he apparently took the position that we could not agree to a universal 50 per cent tariff cut across the board. I think it is fairly obvious why we should not. It must be remembered that throughout the years since the establishment of GATT, as the now Prime Minister said a short time ago in the House of Commons, Canada cooperated fully through all its governments in establishing the GATT principle, and as a result we have a low tariff structure in this country. If, for instance, we have an average tariff structure of 20 per cent and some other country has an average tariff structure of 40 per cent, then in agreeing to a 50 per cent cut we would end up with a 10 per cent average tariff and the other country would still have as high a tariff as we had at the beginning. It is quite obvious
[Mr. Nowlan.l
that some exception will be taken to that, and apparently the minister took such exception.
It is interesting to note, reading back through the discussions which took place in the last few months and years with respect to these negotiations, that there was on the part of the present Prime Minister almost enthusiastic acceptance of the 50 per cent cut across the board. The outcome simply goes to prove what we all know, that on the assumption of responsibility it is much more difficult to carry out airy promises and statements made before one has accepted such responsibility.
The minister has quoted from the chairman's statement at the end as to the compromise arrangement which is to be worked out. That quotation, of course, is reported absolutely objectively and correctly, but he did not quote the interview given by Mr. Christian Herter, who also was in Geneva, and who said these adjustments would only be made-I have forgotten the exact phrase- after proof of tariff and trade imbalances. Everyone knows the difficulty of proving such things. They can go on for years and years, so therefore we can only hope the statement of the chairman is not qualified by the statement made by Mr. Herter at the conclusion of the conference.
So far as we are concerned on this side of the house we of course give full support to any policy which will result in the widening of trade throughout the world, always of course with the reservation that Canada's interests be safeguarded. The Leader of the Opposition took that position when, some time ago, he suggested a conference of like-minded nations to President Kennedy, to accomplish a widening of world trade.
We are appreciative of the statement which the minister has given us this morning. We shall watch with interest the developments and negotiations, and we shall support all logical and proper steps to expand the trade of Canada.

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext:
We in this group have listened with a great deal of interest to the report given by the minister on the two meetings, one in London and the other in Geneva. We endorse the suggestion he has made that we should be looking for a balance of advantage in these tariff negotiations rather than for a straight 50 per cent reduction or any other percentage of reduction.
We hope there will be some follow through of the interest which has been shown rather than paying lip service to the idea of reducing tariffs and then dismissing the subject out of hand, as was done by the previous

government in 1957 when Britain put out a challenge to some of this lip service in favour of tariff reductions. We are pleased to find this emphasis being placed on the development of trade with so-called underdeveloped countries, particularly those within the commonwealth. We in this group believe this is an area where there is the greatest opportunity for trade expansion. We realize that because of the situation which has developed in the United States in the last few days with respect to wheat even more attention will be demanded by this aspect of our agricultural trade.
We wish the minister and his department well in these negotiations and hope they will have the courage to follow through when the items which come up for negotiation reach a point at which some specific action can be taken.

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is to be commended for making a report to parliament so early after his return from attending the two meetings in London and Geneva. I was somewhat disappointed that his report on the commonwealth conference in London dealt with such generalities. I hope we shall have an early opportunity for a fuller discussion of this matter. Certainly the press reports emanating from London gave the impression that the minister, on behalf of Canada, had poured cold water on any idea of a commonwealth trading arrangement. This may not be an accurate report.
We all recognize that a commonwealth trading plan is no substitute for a world trading arrangement. However, it is true that we have very large markets in the commonwealth and particularly in Great Britain, markets which give us a considerable favourable balance in our trading relationships and which help to offset the imbalance in our trade with the United States. It is important that we should retain these markets and, if possible, expand them. While we are waiting for a world trading arrangement, which will undoubtedly take some time to work out, it would seem to the members of this party that no opportunity of strengthening and widening our present trading position within the commonwealth ought to be lost. After all, we cannot keep the commonwealth together merely by airy generalities about a common loyalty to the crown or a common faith in democratic institutions. It will have to be some practical thing which will have meaning particularly for the newly developing nations which have entered the commonwealth and which have serious trading problems at this time.
Report on GATT Conference
With reference to the Geneva conference, it is undoubtedly true that the earlier part of this conference was a great disappointment. The United States insistence on a linear or across the board reduction as against reductions on selected items meant that for a while there was the danger of a complete breakdown. I think the United States position may become less inflexible. If it does not, I am afraid the future prospects for GATT will be considerably dimmed. I hope that at an early date the government will take action to make possible a general debate on this matter so that we may have further information.
I had hoped that in the course of his report to the house the minister would have said something about whether the government is considering the introduction of a trade adjustment act which would set out the kind of compensation to be made available to various segments of our economy which might be adversely affected by tariff adjustments. I think a great deal of uneasiness would be removed if those large areas of our economy which might be affected by tariff adjustments, and other changes which we all recognize will have to be made, knew that legislative and administrative machinery were being provided in order that they might receive some compensation. There would be less uneasiness if they knew there was some period over which the adjustments might be made and that they would be put into effect in an orderly fashion without the dislocation which might follow should action be taken too suddenly.
I think the minister's report has been most useful, but I trust an early opportunity will be presented for fuller discussion so the hon. gentleman might answer questions and give the house further information.

maintopic: GATT-REPORT BY MINISTER ON RESULTS OF CONFERENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think I could be expected to discuss British domestic policy in answer to this question. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Before going on with my remarks I should like to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker on your appointments to your important positions. May I also take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply for their very fine presentations.
I was pleased to hear in the speech from the throne that the government plans to continue the fight against unemployment and will not relax the efforts that have been going on to boost production and co-operate closely with industry. Such promises as a department of industry and an economic council will, I am sure, be welcomed by Canadians as further steps in our continuing battle to provide jobs for as many of our citizens as possible, and to help us to compete with other nations in trade. As you all know, Canada's gross national product last year increased by 7 per cent, a record unsurpassed in the western world, and our record of economic stability was better than that of any other free nation.

The Address-Mr. Weichel You are aware also that employment rose and Canada's external trade reached a record $12.5 billion.
But this fine record, made possible only through co-operation between government and industry, is no reason for us to relax our efforts. We will face growing competition from nations behind the iron curtain which have vowed to bury us in an economic war. The common market countries, now just beginning to flex their muscles, will progressively lower their tariffs and make it tougher for us to sell our goods abroad. During the next three or four years the United States, as a result of Mr. Kennedy's trade bill, will be slashing tariffs in order to compete.
What I mean to emphasize is that with protective tariffs steadily falling in this highly competitive world of the next few years, Canadian producers will have to stand more and more on their own feet. We cannot rest on the records we have chalked up. Instead, we will have to bend our efforts toward devising new ways, new ideas to meet this growing trade challenge.
With this thought in mind, Mr. Speaker, I should like to dwell for a few minutes on a move under way in my constituency of Waterloo North, a move that every community in Canada might do well to copy and a move deserving of support from our new government. I am sure most of you have heard something about it because it received extensive press, radio and television coverage in its initial stage. I am referring to the work going ahead leading to the creation of a labour-management forum to bring about a better understanding between both sides and subsequently boost production and sales.
The plan is to enroll the help of the entire community in the bustling industrial area of Kitchener-Waterloo, where the forum will function, in order to insure its success. Both Mayor Hymen and Mayor Bauer of the two cities agreed, immediately following the first public meeting at which the idea was endorsed, to form a steering committee with respresentatives of labour and management. Two of those directly concerned are George Goebel, president of the Kitchener-Waterloo and district labour council, and Dr. R. V. Yohe, president of B.F. Goodrich Canada Limited. These men have been working quietly but diligently with plans for more public meetings this fall and winter in an effort to put the forum's principles into practice.
Representatives of all segments of the community, including churches, service clubs and other associations, will be joining other delegates from labour and management in discussing common problems and possible solu-

tions. It is hoped that in this way an air of understanding of both sides will begin to permeate through the community. The result, it is expected, will be greater mutual trust and a spirit of co-operation such as is found in European countries.
The founding meeting of this forum, believed to be the first of its kind in North America, drew a crowd of some 700 people in Kitchener. The stimulus for such a get together arose from a Conservative government sponsored mission to Europe last summer. Dr. Yohe, a member of this mission, returned to Canada so impressed with the results of similar projects in Europe that he set about laying the groundwork for a labour management forum in his own community. In fact Dr. Yohe sees such action as almost compulsory for the survival of Canada in this world of competitive trade. I do not believe we can stress too strongly the fact that co-operation among labour, management and government has been the major force in the fantastic post-war economic recovery in Europe.
Of course you might say that conditions in Europe in the years following the war were somewhat different from those existing in Canada today. Their economies were at a standstill, on the verge of collapse, whereas our economy is thriving today. You might say, too, that the widespread despair in postwar Europe was a tremendous stimulus to teamwork and did help to remove prejudice. Here in Canada we have no such despair. However, I feel strongly that the threat of competition we face from other trading nations should be great enough to compel us to forget past prejudices and work together. When Dr. Yohe uses the term "survival" I do not think he is exaggerating. As a member of this national productivity council mission he has visited Europe and has seen what has been accomplished and what competition our products will have to face in the years ahead.
Although we have just completed a banner trade year, not enough of our success has been due to labour-management co-operation. This lack of co-operative spirit so far has made it difficult for our products to compete with those of the European nations in quality, design, price and service. I confess, though, that many of our firms have excellent relations between employer and employee. However, I believe you all know that in many of our industries strife and bitterness between these two factions are deeply rooted and strong. This was equally true in Europe, so the results prove that co-operation is possible if it is seen that survival is at stake.
If we cannot submerge these frictions, which in most cases have prevented labour

and management from working together to cut costs and improve quality, we will have to wage the battle for markets under a severe handicap. I think Dr. Yohe and Mr. Goebel, as well as all the others instrumental in promoting this forum in Kitchener, are to be commended. I feel that the crowd of 700 who turned out for the meeting out of which this forum was born are also to be commended for their interest and foresight.
At the risk of being accused of bragging about my home constituency I suggest it might have been expected that Waterloo North would take the lead role in such a project. The area has a record of stability in industry and business. The people of the constituency are a fine blend of many nationalities and are progressive, hard working folk with a fine record of industrial development. Even during our recession of a few years ago the Kitchener-Waterloo area, one of varied industries, was not hard hit and today enjoys the distinction of being one of the lowest areas of unemployment in Canada.
I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that the Kitchener labour-management forum will bear fruit. I think it is taking the right approach that co-operation in industry is not a government responsibility. This co-operation should start with the worker and his employer. Other communities, I understand, are watching the Waterloo North project closely. They might well follow the Kitchener-Waterloo example by starting at the grass roots with similar forums to hammer out an understanding of how effective co-operation can be developed. At first these forums could function independently of government so that no one could suggest there were any political implications in such projects. However, in the long run government co-operation would be necessary, because I believe all possible resources must be pooled in this fight for economic survival.
I strongly believe, Mr. Speaker, that forums of this kind, aided ultimately by the government, can play a major role in meeting trade competition with other countries. If we properly pursue the objectives outlined for the Kitchener-Waterloo forum I feel that we can not only successfully meet this trade threat, but we can also look forward to higher employment throughout the nation and even a higher standard of living for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks today may I first of all offer you my congratulations on your election to your high office. It is obvious to us all, sir, from the manner in which you have conducted yourself that no mistake was made. The fairness and impartiality you have shown have emphasized this.
The Address-Mr. Temple
I come from the riding of Hastings South in the province of Ontario, an old and historic riding in that province. It is a mixed constituency, rural and urban, containing the city of Belleville, the town of Trenton, the villages of Tweed, Deseronto and Frankford, four rural townships and two large R.C.A.F. bases. Being in that part of the country it is, of course, a beautiful riding. As a matter of fact it cannot escape being so because it adjoins the riding of Northumberland, which is a very fine place indeed.
I was born and raised in the city of Belleville. I am very proud of my home and my constituency, which I hope I shall represent well in this house. I am extremely honoured to be a member of the house. In fact for many years I thought, one might almost say dreamed of participating in the deliberations of the House of Commons, and now I am fully conscious of the honour bestowed on me by the voters in my constituency.
I should like to compliment the Prime Minister, the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon the excellent efforts they are making in the field of trade. This is a matter of great consequence to all ridings and most certainly to Hastings South, because there we produce certain articles and items of such high standards that they can be sold and exported.
In Belleville we have what to us is a large manufacturing plant, the Northern Electric Company, employing some 1,000 people. Recently they have designed a switching system for television networks. It is unique of its kind, has already gone into production, and the first order has been received. The Bata Shoe Company in Batawa produces shoe machinery which is exported to the United States, Australia, Iraq and many other free countries in the world. The Central Bridge Company in Trenton manufactures structural steel and the Stephens-Adamson Company in Belleville are experts in conveying machinery and receive orders from many parts of Canada, the United States and other regions of the world. Of the 115 million pounds of cheese produced in Canada last year, eastern and central Ontario produced almost half. This cheese is a quality product; in fact Canadian cheese can compete anywhere in the world.
So I wish to compliment the new government upon its efforts to expand our trade because, as I say, we do have quality products which must be exported. The reason I stress trade is that over the years we have come more and more toward having one economic class in Canada. We do not have a division of great wealth on the one hand and great poverty on the other, but if we do not expand our trade in this rapidly changing world

The Address-Mr. Aiken we shall again be faced with a great division of wealth, a few people having the vast majority of it and the rest of the population having very little. Should that happen then the state of our democratic institutions can and will suffer.
Like so many other hon. members I am of mixed blood, of mixed racial descent. (Translation):
One of my grandmothers was French speaking; her name was Gariepy. She lived in the big and beautiful city of Montreal. I should add that I too live in a beautiful city.

Mr. Speaker, this government is taking positive and correct steps to improve the economic conditions of Canada, and I look to the day, which I hope is not far off, when we Canadians will consider a university education in the same way we now regard a high school education, as available to all people, based on their ability and application and not on their economic circumstances. We cannot afford to lag behind in this rapidly progressing world, and if we rely on yesterday's knowledge we will end up out of touch with reality.
In conclusion may I say I am certain this government will encourage private initiative. The thing which concerns me more than any other is that as legislation is introduced, both now and over the years to come, it be so carefully scrutinized, as has been the case in this house previously, that no individual liberties will be lost; because if we start losing our individual rights then little by little we shall tend to lose them all and, if we do that, we shall have lost everything.

Before beginning my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend to you my very best wishes and congratulations on assuming the office of our chairman as Speaker, and to congratulate you on the efficient manner in which you have conducted your duties to date. It seems to me that you have not yet had the misfortune to become embroiled in the difficulties your predecessor encountered at the beginning of the last parliament, and I sincerely hope this may continue through the current session.

(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I shall have something to say about the contents of one of these speeches later, but I do congratulate the hon. members for their conciseness and the easy delivery they displayed.
The speech from the throne at the beginning of each session of parliament is an important indication of the intentions of the government. However at the beginning of a new parliament, and especially with a new government, it becomes doubly interesting to carefully examine the speech from the throne in order to find the direction in which the government intends to proceed. We consider the document along with the accompanying speeches and actions to see where it is leading.
This is a comparatively short speech from the throne. That would not in any way detract from its importance if it were concise and to the point. But in this case, after the first 15 paragraphs of generalities, in my opinion the operative part of the speech is directed toward the establishment of boards, commissions and councils without giving those bodies any direction or any indication of what they ought to do. It is possible, of course, that bills will be brought down later to give direction to these organizations, but my primary criticism of this speech is that it announces the intention to set up a large number of boards without indicating the direction in which they are to move. No authority is given to them, and parliament itself has no indication of the course they are to pursue.
I notice that a new department of industry is to be set up. Within it there is to be an area development board, or perhaps a number of such boards. There is to be a new municipal development and loan fund. There is to be a new Canadian development corporation. There is to be a new economic council for Canada. There is to be a division of the Department of Agriculture into two parts and provision for an additional minister. Just imagine the tremendous complex of new government agencies, commissions, boards and councils which will spring up within the framework of the government service when these bodies are established. Imagine the host of employees who will be required to man this new bureaucracy. Perhaps this is the government's answer to the problem of unemployment, to put the unemployed into the government service until the workless figures are substantially reduced. Certainly there is nothing else in the speech from the throne which would directly help to reduce unemployment.
I should like to turn for a moment to the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) when moving the address in reply. I am glad the hon. lady is in the house. Naturally I do not intend to say any-

thing derogatory about her, but I wish to make some comments on her speech because some of the statements she made relate to certain things I have found in the speech from the throne. The hon. lady's remarks were admirably concise and direct. I think they are even more revealing of the philosophy of the party opposite than is the speech from the throne itself. They reveal to me a desire, on her part at least, for a headlong race toward paternalism under a Canadian government. The hon. lady says, in effect, that people are no longer able to make their own decisions and that government must make these decisions for them. In order that I may not inadvertently he misquoting her I should like to read just one paragraph from her speech which seems to me most interesting and which indicates the point I am making. I am reading now from page 22 of Hansard of May 17:
We still hear people talking about the good old days of self-reliant individualism when all an individual had to do was to get up and go. It is always very pleasant to wish we could return to those days; but the fact of the matter is, and we could see this if sometimes we were not blind, that we have moved from an individualist society to a collectivist society, a society where it is very difficult for a great many of us to make the decisions that affect our own destinies. These decisions are increasingly taken by others on our behalf, particularly by large organizations which exist throughout our whole economy. These decisions are simply beyond our control.
As a Conservative member of this house I naturally believe that to take away from the individual the rights which have been built up by society and by the law over the years is a move in the wrong direction. I believe we have to draw a line at the point where the right of decision making by individuals is taken away. That is all I have to say in connection with this address.
There is, however, another question which relates to this. It is the government's quiet move to add thousands of civil servants to the federal payroll. Some of these employees will undoubtedly be required, but I believe the government service is best met by an adequate staff well paid and well protected, rather than by an overpopulated and underpaid public service. There is already an indication of a great expansion in the public service quite apart from the new boards and commissions to which I have referred. This trend, taken together with the large number of boards and councils to be set up as foreshadowed in the speech from the throne and in the light of the remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland in moving the address, indicate to my mind the direction we are taking, a move toward the masterpieces of bureaucracy which the Liberals are so fond of creating, without there being anything new for this great bureaucracy to do.
The Address-Mr. Aiken
I should like now to touch on another subject, namely the question of our relationship with other countries. It has seemed to me that the government is moving rapidly away from the United Kingdom and from the European situation in order to tag along behind the United States. I had the good fortune, shortly after the election, to make a trip to the United States lasting about ten days. I needed a holiday at the time as, no doubt, did most of the other members of this house. I had the opportunity of speaking to a large number of United States citizens, including persons in the government service; and whether they are justified or not, United States citizens believe they won the 1963 elections in Canada and they are waiting now for the country to be delivered to them. This impression was confirmed in their minds by the quick trip which our new Prime Minister made to Washington and the amiable, even eager, approach which was made to the President of the United States.
I believe that international and business relations depend a great deal on mental approach, and the belief by the people of the United States is that the present Leader of the Opposition did not give the American people all they wanted but that the new Prime Minister would give it to them. They believe he was elected on this basis. It is therefore my feeling that the Prime Minister and all members of the government must be exceedingly careful in their relations with the United States to see that this impression does not go beyond the point of no return. This is a thing which gradually begins to grow, and we have seen it growing. We have seen the Prime Minister, when answering questions from time to time, eagerly saying "Yes, I went and discussed this with the President of the United States. Yes, our government is taking this up with the United States. Yes, we are doing everything we can". There is a difference between friendly co-operation and being amiable, and there is very often a misunderstanding of this difference.
While we are the best of friends with the United States as a country, and while the Americans as individuals are the best friends we have-we can all testify to this-we are surely competitors in the business, trade and international arenas. Mr. Speaker, when your competitor comes to you and starts patting you on the back, you must begin to wonder what you are doing wrong. I say that if our United States competitors in world trade keep patting us on the back for any extended length of time, I will begin to wonder what is being given away on behalf of Canada. When we begin to hear a few complaints from across the line, that is when I shall feel a little better

The Address-Mr. Aiken about our relationship with that country. I suggest to the government that they must be on guard; that they have started off from a position they may not be able to get out from under, and I think they have to watch it.
We in Canada have been encouraged to believe, as were the electors at the beginning of the last election campaign and throughout, that mutual friendship and respect, both personal and international, depend upon being amiable with others. This is certainly helpful, but it is only one factor in the situation. Being amiable and friendly does not protect the interests of the persons upon whom you rely, in this case the Canadian people, unless it is accompanied by firm declarations that the interests of your country are to be protected, followed by actions to bring about that result. We have heard that the Prime Minister, while being amiable, friendly, and so on, has also been firm about Canadian rights. 1 do not believe this is true. I believe that up to this point he has been nothing more than amiable and friendly, and I believe this is what has come out of the various meetings. There is nothing wrong with a friendship and a friendly relationship with another country but, Mr. Speaker, the people of this country did not elect a government to give away the heritage that Canada has built up over a great many years.
Accompanying this turning toward the United States is an apparent turning away from the commonwealth. At the beginning of the visit of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the commonwealth conference in London, the newspapers came out with some very strong statements. I have one clipping with me which says that the minister delivered a "blockbuster" to the conference and told them that he was not interested in commonwealth trade at all, that he was interested purely in an over-all trade pattern, and that the commonwealth as such was not very much good.
As we have seen today from the statement of the minister and the very direct comments made by the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), it is very easy to make these general statements on trade. It is very easy to say that we will cut tariffs 50 per cent across the board. But it is not so easy when you come to consider the individual interests of the Canadian people. We have over the years built up a very unusual complex of industry and agriculture in this country. It is one which is not easy to sell. We have a good standard of living. We have high wages, or at least reasonably high wages. We have difficulty in competing with foreign countries, particularly those countries where the wage standard is very low. Over the years we have

built up a pattern of trade. We have negotiated time and again in GATT and in other international arenas for the protection of these industries which are Canada's and those agricultural commodities which Canada grows and exports.
It is not possible immediately to enter the picture and say that all that is going to be changed; it just cannot be done, Mr. Speaker. While any government comes into power with great ideas and expressions of opinion, I hope the present government will quickly come down to the facts of life which have been learned by governments in the past, and which this government learned before 1957. We find upon our front benches several members of the previous administration. They knew full well what our problems were. They knew full well that the former government was dealing with them effectively. In order to get elected hon. members opposite had to criticize, granted; but I do believe that unless they face reality and get over their desire to be friendly with everybody and give everybody everything they want, we in Canada are going to face some very severe times ahead.

Mr. Speaker, it is not given to all new members to have the opportunity to speak twice during the course of the throne speech debate. However, I am very gratified that a technicality of procedure allows me to make some further remarks. I should like to express my very deep gratitude to my colleagues who, by allowing me to take their place, have afforded me the opportunity of informing the house and the nation about a situation with regard to which I feel very strongly. I refer to Bell island, which is in my district of St. John's East.
Bell island is a community of 14,000 people, and the tragic fact is that of those 14,000 the staggering number of 5,500 are on relief. They are existing, not living. Their fathers and grandfathers before them made a decent, if frugal, living; but these men and women of today in Canada cannot. Wabana is a one industry town. There are only the great iron mines to provide these people with the jobs they need to support them. These mines have been producing the rich red iron ore ever since 1896, and uncounted millions of tons have been torn from the mines. These mines run three or four miles out under the waters of beautiful Conception bay. The reddish dust which covers every single object on Bell island is famed throughout Newfoundland, and the ore which produces this dust has been the bread and butter of many of our people these 70 years now. However, lately Wabana has fallen on hard times.

I am not an expert in these matters, sir, and I do not pretend to be one. I do not understand why these hard times have come. All I know is that the far flung overseas markets seem to have gone away, and the jobs have gone with them. I fear they have gone forever. But the people have not gone, and only this week it was announced that yet another 150 miners would be laid off. Some 5,500 out of 14,000 are on dole, and there will be still more in this Canadian twentieth century.
The company which employs these men no longer finds it economically feasible to offer work, so they are left to shift for themselves. Bell islanders and their forebears have worked this mine for 70 years. The succession of companies that has employed these men in my opinion did precious little to improve the community that housed them. Their only interest over the years, it would seem to me, was to get the ore out of the ground as cheaply as possible. They spent a mere tuppence on the miners, their families and the town. I would not want to write the epitaph of the companies that operated these mines. They have never felt any real sense of obligation to the community that gave them many years of pecuniary gain. As a result Wabana has bred a fiercely independent type of men, proud men, who are humbled at the thought of what lies ahead.
There is no single community in Newfoundland so deserving of whatever constructive policy this house may have to offer. They have nowhere else to turn. They ask us for a helping hand. In past years when these men were working they made a magnificent contribution to Newfoundland's never too prosperous economy. In war and peace they have stood with the finest men of this country. They have given me the great responsibility of being their spokesman in this house. They look to this house, through me, to offer them something more than mere soothing words.
This government has introduced an imaginative and progressive program which will help Canada generally. I have no doubt of that. But, Mr. Speaker, what will this mean to my people of Bell island? How can these policies be translated into action for Wabana, which is an Indian name for "land of the rising sun"? I am not criticizing anyone and I am not blaming anyone, because it may be that there is no blame. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is a national shame which should burn into the heart of every Canadian. Mr. Speaker, you may very well say "Why do these people live on Bell island? Why do they not leave?" But where can they go? Must these people tear themselves away from the homes that have been theirs for generations
The Address-Mr. O'Keefe and go elsewhere? This twentieth century which is Canada's must hold more than this for our people.
What is to be done? I do not know; I wish to God I did. But this I can say, sir, and I say it with all the force I can muster, with all the strength that is in my body and with all the fervour that is in my soul. Something should be done, and I -hope that something will be done.
The fact that governmental expenditure may have avoided actual privation and may have even given a boom aspect to sections of our economy cannot conceal the existence of a very high level of unemployment. This has two effects. First, the provincial economy loses millions of dollars in production through the enforced idleness of thousands of its workers, and second all those who are supported by any form of government aid are adding to the load of the people who are gainfully employed. Our province of fewer than half a million, with the lowest level of per capita income in Canada and an enormous territory to administer, cannot be expected to find easy solutions to all these problems.
I believe that any region of Canada which is at this time afflicted with a high rate of unemployment should join forces with a Canada-wide planning association or organization. This should be set up to assist the provinces. This kind of federal-provincial co-operation is, I suggest, essential to national and regional progress. While certain it is that Newfoundland's needs are great and many, it is just as certain that our prospects for the future are indeed bright. Our dynamic premier's list of projects which he hopes to see achieved, as does every Newfoundlander and every Canadian, is indeed challenging and imaginative.
Were I to mention at this time only one, I would have to choose the dramatic development of the vast hydro potential of the Hamilton watershed in Newfoundland, Labrador. Estimates of what can be produced vary from 4 million to 7 million horsepower. Even at the lowest figure this enterprise is immense; it is gigantic by any standard. It would be clearly advantageous to Quebec, to Newfoundland and indeed to Canada as a whole if this power could be fed into a Quebec grid, when power now utilized in Quebec could be released for delivery to Ontario and for export to the United States.
What is certain is that the resources of the province of Newfoundland are now better known than ever before, and that the wishful thinking about them in the past has been converted into actual developments of great magnitude and into prospects which must in time become the source of new production and employment on a substantial

The Address-Mr. O'Keefe scale. With our rapidly increasing population and costs it will be badly needed in our province.
In that vein, sir, I do not wish to be considered insular or parochial, we are now part of a nation that is great and growing in stature. To us has been committed the destiny of that great nation. It is for us- and I speak particularly to newer members like myself-to realize that in the economic growth and expansion of Canada lies the successful development of all the areas which form its component parts. In that sense may I appeal for a broader outlook in our discussions and an awareness of national problems and their over-all importance. In my opinion, now more than ever before Canada's great need is unity, unity of thought, unity of action and unity of effort.
Perhaps because I am new to the scene I have found great difficulty in accepting or even understanding the dissensions and divisions about which we hear so much.

Mr. Speaker, during the last election a good deal of nonsense was indulged in about anti-Americanism. There is hardly a family in the maritimes that cannot visit a relative in what are colloquially know as the "Boston states". It seems almost trite to disclaim anti-Americanism. No nation carrying such harrowing world wide responsibilities as does the United States should be subject to anything but constructive comment and criticism. Canada has unique political military and economic problems which should be appreciated by United States politicians. Now that the election is over I presume United States newspapers and periodicals will resume their massive ignoring of Canada, although perhaps a helpful side-effect of the NATO meeting will be that some newspapermen will find us interesting and our affairs worth commenting upon. Many Canadians were disappointed by the total disregard in the throne speech of any mention of the problems facing our universities. The previous government has an enviable record in aid to universities-first, by increasing the grants per student enrolled and, second, by including dormitory construction under long term C.M.H.C. loans.
Adjectives and superlatives abound about university problems but in most instances are not used in exaggeration. "Crisis" was the word used in 1961; "staggering" was how the Canadian Universities Foundation described its analysis of financial requirements on operating and capital account for the foreseeable future. Total university expenditure in 1960-1961 was $282 million. That estimated in 1965-1966 is $692 million. The plan for university scholarships is commendable but will only touch half the problem. Flying on one wing, someone has termed the plan. In fact, a scheme for scholarships

without immediate and generous federal assistance to both capital and current costs of educating the students would be a menace and not a help. I suggest that every dollar for scholarships should be matched by a dollar paid to the university to help with overhead costs. This will not end federal responsibility. Mr. Speaker, both in Britain and Canada attention is being focused on the role of parliament and its members in the contemporary scene. Mr. J. Grimond, leader of the Liberal party in the United Kingdom, says it is not as if the House of Commons had been handed down by God; it should be reformed.
Dean James A. Gibson of Carleton University in an address to the Ottawa chapter of the Canadian public relations society made several suggestions which I will merely list. One of these was mentioned by our leader the other day. The first was a permanent voters list, which would be an obvious advantage and is long overdue. Second, he suggested smaller parliamentary committees with expert staffs. As Dean Gibson says, the opportunities for a backbench private member to become well briefed on subjects of national concern are inadequate and much neglected. Third, he recommended an agreement by the parties as to how much time should be allotted to debates on particular topics. Fourth -and I think this is a very interesting one and should be of concern particularly to government benches-debates on public questions which are the deliberate concern of parliament should take place in the House of Commons and not on television or radio. And last, fuller, more informative and more genuine reporting to the people of Canada by all the official delegations which go abroad, including reporting on their extra-curricular visits. I am told, by the way, that everyone who had an extra-curricular visit to Paris last year was returned, which is a measure of the maturity of Canadian electors.

Mark Bonham Carter, writing in the Guardian of March 14, 1963, said that there are three questions-and I think these questions apply to us-to be answered. Is parliament efficient? Does it control our governors'-* Is it representative of the country as a whole? I am afraid we must share the answer which was given in England and say that the answer is almost certainly no. An hon. member must, in my opinion, have access to information and this should be provided by availability of expert staffs and through specialized committees.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we are being bombarded these days by new and convenient interpretations of the constitution, most of them under the guise of a formula to make confederation work. Some of these statements show a singular lack of appreciation for the objectives of the British North America Act.
I think it will not do us harm if we remind ourselves that Sir John A. Macdonald and his colleagues designed the act of confederation expressly to avoid the narrowness of the states rights provisions of the United States constitution. The statesmen of Sir John's day knew all about the American document and a study of the debates prior to confederation shows the length to which our constitution-makers went to avoid the narrowness of the United States constitution, which is being shown today in the state of Alabama. Canada has been ill-served in the intervening years by narrow and restrictive interpretations of the B.N.A. Act. I suggest that when we here chart a course to help Quebec and her culture reach their undoubted place within the confederation, we recall the days of 100 years ago. Perhaps that could be our contribution to our centenary. It is not so much the document which is at fault, but the spirit with which it has been interpreted since its enactment. Surely there can be no Canada without Quebec; neither can there be Quebec without Canada.

In the speech from the throne we have a very brief reference to agriculture. It has been pointed out that we are now to have two ministers of agriculture, one from the east and one from the west. I do not know whether this is the best policy. I question whether it is. The trouble is that in the past, under the former Liberal administration and the Conservative administration, we have had a patchwork set-up as far as agriculture is concerned. We have had not just two policies but a great many policies. I remember that when I had the opportunity of representing the Fraser Valley a number of years ago I called the attention of the government to the fact that certain overriding policies must be laid down as far as agriculture is concerned. I recognize the fact, of course, that separate areas have separate problems and perhaps special consideration will have to be given to those areas, but I also believe we must have certain policies that apply right across the nation. Unless we have these we are not going to have that unity which has been the subject of so much discussion in this house.
I listened with interest to the hon. member from Wentworth (Mr. Morison) when he was participating in the debate yesterday. He referred to the lucky western farmers. He went on to say that, contrary to the lucky western farmers, the farmers in his area were caught in the cost-price squeeze. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is one problem that applies right across the nation. From coast to coast those in this great primary

producing industry, agriculture, are faced with this same problem. It has been pointed out on some occasions that the income of farmers has increased. However, when one takes into consideration the constantly increasing costs of production there is not very much to brag about. This applies to those in eastern Canada as well as those in western Canada. Therefore I would suggest that this matter be given very serious consideration, as I believe it will, in order that agriculture may move up the scale and occupy that place in our economy that it should occupy. I would urge that it receive its fair share of the income of this great nation of ours.
There is a reference in the speech from the throne to the development of a national fisheries policy. This is also a very important matter. The fisheries, as well as agriculture, is a very important matter as far as my own constituency is concerned. Certainly as far as British Columbia is concerned the fisheries is one of our great industries. Those engaged in the fishing industry, and the representatives of the fisheries organizations, are very apprehensive of the trends and developments relating to this industry. I have received through the mail a number of communications with respect to this matter and to the amendments to the international north Pacific fisheries treaty. I think these organizations were perfectly within their rights when they requested that these matters be referred to the parliamentary committee on marine and fisheries before they were given approval by the cabinet. Instead of that however, the cabinet has apparently seen fit to go ahead and approve these amendments without having them taken under advisement by the committee, and without giving these organizations an opportunity of making representations.
In this connection, I wish to refer to a letter from the Hon. Earle C. Westwood, minister of recreation, conservation and fisheries for British Columbia. This letter was addressed to the Hon. J. Angus MacLean, who was then our minister of fisheries. It states:
As minister of fisheries for the province of British Columbia herewith my request that implementation of the recommendations and decisions of the Canadian section of the international north Pacific fisheries commission pertaining to the decisions re abstention zones reached at the commission's 1962 annual meeting held in Seattle, November 17, 1962 be subject to examination by the federal standing committee on marine and fisheries.
Such consideration and hearings before the standing committee on marine and fisheries will permit opportunity for those concerned to submit briefs on the recommendations and decisions of the Canadian section of the commission before these recommendations are brought to the floor of the House of Commons.

Apparently he was rather optimistic when he thought it would go that far. He then proceeds to give the reasons for this particular request. Before the last parliament was dissolved we had a full delegation from the united fishermen and allied workers' union who presented this matter to the various groups in this house for consideration. Mr. Speaker, this is not a very good way to promote public relations. It is not a very good way to promote understanding between the various groups which make up our economy, and the legislative bodies. I trust that with all speed this committee will be set up and will have the opportunity of studying not only those amendments, which consideration may be now too late, but also other suggestions and recommendations which those interested in this industry can present.
The speech from the throne contained reference to municipal financing problems. This is a matter that was given great consideration by the members of this particular group. We have insisted that if we are going to solve our problems we have to solve the problem of municipal financing. We have recommended the establishment of a municipal development bank, as a branch of the Bank of Canada, to make loans to municipalities at the cost of administration. This has been taken up by some of the other foups- They will not follow, of course, the formula that we suggest, but nevertheless we appreciate the fact that recognition is given to the problem and they are willing to consider this particular matter.
I wonder if this proposal will share the same unfortunate fate that befell the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act some years ago. Under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act of 1938 loans could be made to municipalities at a rate of interest of 2 per cent. In Hansard of October 24, 1957, page 389 we have the record of questions in this connection raised by the late Mr. Tom Irwin of this group. He was advised that all loans were discontinued after December 31, 1940, and no applications have since been entertained. Up to that time 143 applications for loans were received of which 110 were approved. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that this act was passed in 1938 but after 1940 no further applications for loans were entertained.
I wonder why the Liberal party put a stop to that particular program. I wonder why they ceased to make loans under that act. Quite a few years have lapsed but now they
The Address-Mr. Herridge come along with the suggestion-I do not know whether or not the rate of interest is going to be 2 per cent-that they are going to set up a municipal loan fund of some description. I hope it does not share the fate of the one that was established in 1938.
Another matter to which a number of members have made reference is the question of the Columbia development. We look forward with a great deal of anticipation to an early and favourable conclusion of the negotiations now going on with respect to this project. Liberal governments have not acted with any great degree of alacrity in the past with respect to the development of this great source of power. For many years it was under consideration but that is as far as it got. It was a Liberal government that blocked the plan some years ago to develop this system and it is questionable if any plan considered since that time has been any more advantageous than the one proposed then.
The Prime Minister now promises to renegotiate the treaty, but we hope this will not result in several more decades of delay and frustration. I am not going to say that no changes should be made. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) stated today, I believe, that it is difficult for a layman to understand all the ins and outs of this great problem. I simply voice the hope that the negotiations may be concluded speedily and that we will be able to proceed with this great project that will mean so much not only to the province of British Columbia but to the whole nation as well.
There are many matters with which I wish to deal, including quite a number of problems relating to my own constituency, but opportunities will be afforded on future occasions and I will reserve my remarks on them until then.

I am sure you have the good will of the whole house. I know that principles of justice and fair play endure throughout the centuries and I want to say, Mr. Speaker that I trust when time steals your years away and you come to the end of your Speaker's day you will be able to use the words of Solon, the father of Athenian democracy, in about the seventh century before Christ and say with him:

I cannot proceed with my remarks without congratulating the mover (Miss Jewett) and seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. There is a growing awareness among members of the house of the need for improvement of the machinery of parliament to meet changing circumstances and conditions. This question will be dealt with at much greater length by members of this group and other members of the house, I am quite confident, but I wish to take this opportunity to make a few observations as a result of some recollections in solitude.
With respect to the Senate, I am not going into the question of abolition and reform and that sort of thing. However I do think that good work has been done by committees of the Senate in recent years, particularly by the committee on manpower and the committee on land use, and in my view this good work indicates that the government could use the committees of the Senate to much greater advantage. I suggest that the government give consideration to utilizing the committees of the Senate to carry on certain investigations and inquiries such as are at present given to royal commissions. I think in doing that the government will put these matters in the hands of competent persons and there will be a considerable saving to the public exchequer.
A word or two with respect to the House of Commons. I welcome the reference in the throne speech to the establishment of a committee on procedure under the chairmanship of Mr. Speaker to strengthen, as the words read, and make parliament more effective. In my opinion the committee should give consideration to the length of speeches in order to provide an opportunity for as many members as possible to participate in this type of debate and especially in the committee of the whole house. I think that on occasion speeches are too lengthy and we could save time and
[Mr. Herridge.l
provide opportunities for more to participate when the house is in committee.
I think there should be more consideration given to the organization and efficiency of committees, their hours of sitting and so on.
I think the government should give consideration to the necessity of a research staff available to members of parliament. I trust that consideration will be given to this matter. Then, there is another reason for moving the Sergeant-at-Arms to the centre, which I think should even be more convincing. Our leader has very well expressed our response to the items in the throne speech. He has dealt fully with our attitude to the problems that face us today. I am going to confine my remarks from this point on to one very serious and important question, namely, the development of the Columbia river. The Columbia river treaty was signed by the representatives of the governments of Canada and of the United States in Washington on January 17, 1961. Ratification was approved by the United States senate with

only a few minutes of discussion, and with only one dissenting vote, on March 2, 1961. The treaty has not been presented to the Canadian parliament for consideration.
However, Mr. Speaker, the terms of this document have been available to the people of Canada for more than two years, and the result has been a growing understanding of the terms of the treaty as well as the disastrous effect on the rights and vital interests of our country. Many qualified engineers and other persons have given this treaty very careful study from an objective point of view and, as a consequence many organizations and individuals have expressed their opposition to the terms of the treaty. I should like to list some of them briefly in order to indicate to the house the strength of the opposition and the quality of that opposition to this treaty.
First of all, I must mention General Mc-Naughton. I should like to refer hon. members to press reports of his speeches to the Canadian institute of engineering, the Alberta engineering institute and to his articles in magazines and newspapers. Then, there is Mr. F. J. Bartholomew, electrical engineer, Vancouver, B.C., a very well known consulting engineer; Mr. Richard Deane, electrical engineer, for Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, Rossland, B.C.; Larrett Higgins, Toronto, Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission; J. M. Southin, a very well known British Columbia Conservative and registered professional electrical engineer. He said that this is a treaty we could very well do without. Then, I should like to mention the B.C. convention of the New Democratic party, all the trade unions in British Columbia and many unions in other parts of Canada; and the chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia.
In that connection, I should like to refer to a recent incident. You know, a very well known gentleman, Dr. Keenleyside, came to Nelson just before the election. He was invited to speak at a public event there. Then, he had a reception afterwards and some of my friends were at that reception. He took the opportunity to discuss the Columbia treaty and to point out that if it were not signed this year there would not be any treaty signed at all because the United States were getting impatient. He expressed some disappointment at the support the hon. member for Kootenay West was receiving for his views. He urged action to promote early ratification of the treaty. As a result the Nelson chamber of commerce, at the annual meeting of the associated chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia, on April 5 and 6 presented a resolution urging immediate ratification of the Columbia river
The Address-Mr. Herridge treaty. This was the subject of debate and there were some very qualified engineers and others at that meeting. As a result of that debate, the resolution urging immediate ratification of the present Columbia river treaty was defeated 33 to 15. The advisory board of the farmers institute of British Columbia have opposed it. Dear Mr. Waterfield:
Your letter of April 12th has just arrived and I would like to assure you that I agree with you that it is imperative to renegotiate the Columbia river treaty.
