7.	Shortly after the treaty was signed, Premier Bennett wished the treaty terms altered to provide the sale of downstream benefits on a firm and long term basis. We have witnessed some interesting reversals of policy at high levels with regard to the proposed development of the Columbia river.
8.	During the discussions on the international rivers bill in 1955 attorney general Bonner and water controller Paget expressed strong opposition to the flooding of the Arrow lakes. This policy was reversed when they came to deal with the present Columbia river treaty.
9.	In the years past, the present Leader of the Opposition opposed the idea of the long term export of firm power, then reversed his position according to the throne speech of September last. I want to indicate how completely the hon. gentleman reversed his position, and I quote from page 3

of a statement made by the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada, following the signing of the Columbia river treaty in Washington. This is what he said about the treaty:
So far as Canada is concerned, the most important feature of the treaty is the one I have already referred to-the recognition of the principle of division of downstream benefits. From that principle all the great advantages that are possible for Canada as a result of co-operative development of the Columbia basin flow. Without that principle the entire arrangement would be fruitless for this country.
This is the bedrock upon which the treaty is supposed to stand, but afterwards they hurled that great arrangement overboard.
10.	Mr. Fulton, chief negotiator for Canada, opposed the long term sale of downstream benefits in the most vehement language, and then reversed his position.
11.	It is obvious from these reversals of policy, on the part of those who are supposed to know what they were talking about, that this present treaty was entered into with undue haste without understanding all of its terms and their consequence, or without the facts with respect to problems and costs of construction, rehabilitation, compensation or the unnecessary destruction of natural resources.
However, as the facts have come to light throughout the months, we can view this delay as a blessing in disguise.
I now submit a quotation from the speech of Professor Marts, professor of geography, Washington University, at the Kelowna natural resources conference in August 1962.
Canada should resist pressure to hurry a decision from any group including the United States and make certain that their final decision will be a correct one and not regretted at a later date. Canada would be well advised to make haste slowly on the Columbia river development.
This present delay presents an opportunity to the government for the first time to do some effective planning for the development of the water resources of the Columbia river to the advantage of Canada and with equity for the United States. Therefore, on behalf of this party, I suggest the following, and let me say I am trying to be as non-partisan as possible in this. I admit I have a sentimental interest in this question because I live in that country, know its beauty and love its land, waters and beaches. I make these proposals:
1.	That the Canadian government inform the United States government and the government of British Columbia that the proposed treaty is not satisfactory.

2.	That re-negotiation be commenced on the basis of the adoption of the principles for development adopted by the international joint commission.
3.	That the government proceed on the basis that sequence 9 (a) is the most acceptable plan for Canada.
4.	That we propose a flexible approach for the timing and staging of developments to fit the load curve. That we should begin the building of the Mica creek dam first in order to provide flood control protection to Canada and the United States.
5.	We propose the development of Dorr dam in order to satisfy primary flood control in the United States.
6.	We urge the appointment of General McNaughton as chief adviser to the Canadian government negotiating team.
7.	We urge that, prior to any final decision, public hearings be held in east and west Kootenay by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) according to the powers provided by the terms of the International Rivers Act. There is nothing like having these questions fairly discussed and presented to the people concerned. The hearings should not be held in a courtroom atmosphere where ordinary citizens are made to feel small and cheap, and uninformed. They should be held in the usual way such hearings have been conducted by the federal government throughout the years.
8.	Then the result of the discussions and evidence presented at the public hearings in east and west Kootenay should be referred to the external affairs committee, when it is studying a proposed treaty.
We suggest that this procedure will do the following:
1.	Provide opportunity to obtain advice and opinions from qualified persons.
2.	Provide an opportunity for organizations and persons in the area affected to be informed and their views heard, whether they are farmers, village residents, industrial workers, tourist operators and so on.
3.	Provide the government and members of the external affairs committee with essential information upon which to base any decision.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have hurried through this very complex and very complicated subject, but I have presented it in such a way so that it would be somewhat easy to digest by those who do not live in the area and are not acquainted with all the developments. Before concluding, and in order that they may get all the available information before they deal with this matter in the house, I suggest all hon. members get copies of a statement on the proposed Columbia river treaty made to senators and members of parliament in the
The Address-Mr. Ethier House of Commons on Wednesday, December 12, 1962 at a meeting presided over by joint chairmen, the hon. member for Kootenay East and the hon. member for Kootenay West. This statement was made by General McNaughton. I also suggest they get a copy of an address given by General McNaughton to the association of professional engineers of Alberta held at Calgary on March 23, 1963.
I further suggest they get the latest issue of the International Journal, spring 1963, which costs 75 cents a copy. I see my colleague from Toronto has already got a copy of it, as have other hon. members. They will find a very complete article in it on the proposed Columbia treaty, by General A. G. L. McNaughton, which is very informing, covering the legal, engineering and economic aspects of the treaty. I also suggest they get a copy of the Engineering and Contract Record for September 1962 in which they will find an article on the Columbia treaty. Then too I suggest they would be well advised to get, from the Department of External Affairs, the
report of the international joint commission__
United States and Canada-on principles for determining and apportioning benefits from co-operative use of storage of waters and electrical interconnection within the Columbia river system. It is, sir, a pleasure and an honour for me to be able to participate in this very important throne speech debate. I know there is a tendency in the press and elsewhere to denigrate this particular part of our parliamentary proceedings. I hear the expression that the throne speech debate drones on and interest slackens. Actually, the parliament of Canada is not designed for the amusement of the press gallery. It is of the utmost importance that this legislative chamber remain always a representative body and that we have the viewpoints constantly put forward of those members who are elected from various parts of this country. I think it is a vital and highly necessary part of our proceedings.
I would like to begin, as hon. members who preceded me have begun, in congratulating our Speaker and Deputy Speaker. I would like to say a particular word to the deputy chairman of committees. It is some time since one of our chief presiding officers has come from the Atlantic provinces, and I wish the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) all good wishes in the discharge of his duties.
There are those in this country who are concerned about the permanency of the speakership, and this indeed may be a forward step. But as I have looked back over the record of Canadian history I am not convinced that this high office has been degraded by the hon. gentlemen who have held it through the years. I would like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This is not only a perfunctory duty; it is a real pleasure. I congratulate especially the mover, who is a fellow political scientist; indeed, a professor of political science. It would probably be ungracious of me to use the expression "egghead" about such a charming lady, although I have been the
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie recipient of the expression many, many times in the house. But it is for me, perhaps, a more appropriate expression. I think we do well to have a few academicians among the hidebound or practical politicians who make up the bulk of those in this chamber. I would like to say that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) indulged in a bit of poetic licence today when he spoke about his constituency being the Garden of Eden. I speak a straight line when I say that I represent the garden province of Canada, the garden of the gulf or, perhaps, in deference to the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) I should say that I represent the most prosperous and most beautiful and politically perceptive part thereof.
I was impressed, too, by the speech of the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Ethier) and I congratulate him on something I have long sought but have been unable to obtain, his felicity and facility in both languages. If I sought to give him any advice it would not be in languages, but I would say that when it comes to cheese, if he wants to be a gourmet he should try Tyne Valley, Prince Edward Island. I think the mover made a most interesting contribution to the debate and I think my good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) followed that approach today, in that he and she before him looked at some of the fundamentals upon which our political system is based and examined some of the organizations and institutions of Canadian politics. She, I believe, pointed out that because of her observations and study of the Liberal party she decided to become a Liberal. I would not want to indulge in too much selfconfession, but I went through a similar performance and I made a somewhat different choice. I had long been convinced of the great contribution made by the political group that was founded by Sir John A. Macdonald over 100 years ago. I knew he had been impressive in his stand for a strong national policy, that he had shown moderation in days of extremism, that he brought a pragmatic and sound approach to problems facing this difficult, challenging and wonderful country. As I looked over our political history I saw the same emphasis on a sound and vigorous nationalism personified by that great Nova Scotian, that great Canadian, Robert Borden, who was the chief architect of Canada's independent nationhood, the man who said, "If you want our aid, call us to your councils"' and who was not unprepared to accept all the responsibilities which were given to this country. Then I thought of one of the series of great Conservatives in the long story of our party, the late Arthur Meighen, who typified forthrightness and a straightforward

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie meeting of even the most thorny issues, and a refusal to deal in the kind of indirect discourse and opinion-reading which sometimes brings success to the shrewd politician but apparent failure to the statesman.
However, the moment of truth came when as a Canadian voter I sat in the gallery of this House of Commons and saw the frightening drama of the pipe line debate. I saw closure brutally applied. I saw our parliamentary institution shaken to its very foundation. Then I decided to put all else aside and give such energy and ability as I might possess to the party which fought against that terrible threat to our democratic institution. I am proud to say-and I am not one of those who believe that one party has a monopoly of all the virtues-that in the six years in which I supported the government never once did I see it resort to such repressive tactics no matter how sustained or fractious the oposition. I cannot but note that some who sat in the seats of power in those days sit there again.
But enough of the past. We hope those days are gone and that those who are now in government will not even be tempted ever to return to that kind of conduct. Perhaps this is what is meant in the throne speech when we find the expression, "Familiar ways of thought and action are becoming less certain guides". We now have, if not the new era at least a new parliament, a government in office but barely in power. We have a large, active, vigorous opposition. These are things from which one can take some comfort. I believe that the April 8 election has done something; it has expressed the Canadian people's preference for the two-party system, and I believe that before too long the third and fourth parties will disappear from our political spectrum. The New Democratic party was something of a marvel in our age. Never was there a party so long aborning, never such elaborate birth rites, and yet it seems to have gone into a decline before it reached its adolescence.

speechtext:
Of the Social Credit party I will say nothing. They, I believe, have troubles enough of their own. But what of the new government, still enjoying a political honeymoon, still basking in the glaring light of favourable publicity? How soon, I ask, will the cracks in its fagade become apparent? How quickly will its great list of tremendous promises and magnificent commitments run it into difficulties, difficulties dire and dreadful, I am afraid?
Much is said of the ability of the new administration, and I hope for Canada that these men who form it are as able as their friends proclaim. Yet I cannot forbear to

feel that in this new government we have seen administrative ability and expertise become the leading virtues. An efficient and effective bureaucracy is essential in the modern state but the bureaucracy is the means of government. It must never itself become the government. Sound judgment, awareness of the needs of all parts of the country and, above all, an ever-present sensitivity to the parliamentary process and the democratic fundamentals are much, much more important. I sincerely hope that the Prime Minister will never allow these priorities to be lost sight of. As an old professor of mine used to say, experts should be on tap but never on top. This man was a good Liberal too, and there are lots of good Liberals in the universities.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am not disposed to be critical. I believe that Canadians as a whole want to see this government given a chance because they may feel its tenure may not be very long. Yet even at this stage I have one disappointment. I had thought that my long time friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), would have been a little more prominent in the early 60-day decisive phase of the government. He did not go to London, nor did he go to Hyannis Port. Nor has he in these early decisive days been able to bring about his cherished desire of bringing Canada into the organization of American states. I thought he might be making some tours in Latin America when his Prime Minister was going to Massachusetts and London, but I have not heard that we are moving into the organization of American states.
But I remember what I heard last January. The hon. member who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs said then:
The time was never more urgent for us to accept the longstanding invitation of every member of the O.A.S. and to join this organization.
1 have been looking forward to such a step for many years and I thought he was the man who would finally lead us to accept some of our hemispheric responsibilities. But not even in the speech from the throne do I detect the slightest hint that this step is about to be taken. However, I wish the new Secretary of State for External Affairs well. Never would I accuse him of doing anything to injure Canada's prestige abroad or to lower our standing among the international community. I am equally convinced that the same would be said by every objective Canadian about the two great statesmen who preceded him, the late Sidney Smith and the Hon. Howard Green.
If there was one thing about the last election campaign which I think should soon be forgotten and pass into the limbo of things

which should never be uttered in campaigns, it was the suggestion by spokesmen of the present government that Canada's repute abroad was being lowered. This was positively not the case, and Canada's role in the last six years offers far more eloquent refutation than I could ever give.
I was impressed and pleased with and I congratulate the new member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) upon the remarks he made about the Hon. Howard Green. They were a little in contradiction of some of the things said by some of his political associates during the recent campaign.
But I think this is not a time to dwell on negatives, Mr. Speaker. I think all hon. members will want to assist the new government in its difficult task, and if they do not think they are going to have difficulties they have a rude awakening not far ahead. We are interested in seeing what they will do, in seeing how they will translate into positive and meaningful action the commitments which in such large measure they gave the people of Canada from coast to coast. I should like to presume to assist the new ministers with particular reference to the province of Prince Edward Island.
I think Prince Edward Island makes a good test case. In no province is the question of dominion-provincial relations so important and I think that a dominion government which does well by Prince Edward Island can measure up to discharge its duties properly for the whole of Canada. One fundamental problem in Prince Edward Island is the problem which was germane to the confederation discussions of 1873, that of transportation. We were a bit reluctant to enter confederation-when I say "we" I am speaking historically-and we insisted that efficient and continuous communication with the mainland must be guaranteed by the dominion government.
If you go down through the years you will find that Prince Edward Island members of parliament, whether Liberal or Conservative-we have never had any other kind- have asked about the honouring and the upgrading of this commitment with regard to the question of transportation. It is a vital question. More and more people are showing their good judgment and coming to our island province. They are coming by the thousands and they are welcome. There is room, and the happy thing about it is that those who come return again and again.
Hon. members will recall we have discussed the question of ferries. When the Liberal party came into power in 1935 it found at Borden two ferries, one four years old and one 18 years old. After 22 years in office they left at Borden two ferries, one 10 years old
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie and the other 40 years old. When the last government left office a few weeks ago there were at Borden four ferries on the run or available on the run and plans were under way for yet another new one. So I would say to the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith), who is not here, along with most of the members of his party, that this is a fundamental thing for him to consider and that he has quite a challenge to meet if he is going to live up to the record of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) when he was minister of transport.
I was interested when the minister replied to my colleague, the senior member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), the other day in respect of the building of a new ferry for the Borden-Tormentine run and said that plans are going forward. I should like them to go forward at an even faster rate. I very much hope that the decision to build this ferry, coupled with the lack of reference to the causeway in any official announcement by the government, does not mean that the present government will repudiate the commitment of its predecessor in respect of the building of this tremendous land link which will finally join Canada and Prince Edward Island. I should like to make it very clear that we do not consider the causeway to be one of those projects to be decided upon by the Atlantic development board, no matter how many members it is going to have on it. In the first place, $100 million would not build the causeway and, even more important, this is a great project which has already been decided upon and upon which we received a commitment which I expect will be fulfilled.
Then, I should like to deal with the question of fiscal needs. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) were here, I could point out to him the success story of the last government in the way it dealt with our little province. During the fiscal year 1956-57 Prince Edward Island received $4,870,000 from Ottawa. During the fiscal year 1961-62 the amount was $12,242,000. Total expenditures by Ottawa on behalf of Prince Edward Island were, for the corresponding years, $30,569,000 and $47,394,000. This is the kind of pattern we expect him to emulate because if he does not, to plagiarize the title of a well known book, he will have a sorely troubled Prince Edward Island on his hands.
We recall with appreciation how quickly the former government moved to implement the Atlantic Provinces Adjustment Act. This made great new sources of revenue available to our province and to our sister provinces in the maritimes to extend further the services needed by our people.

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie
II the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) were here, I would say to him that we hope he will emulate his three predecessors in their vigour and their interest in the development of one of the finest national parks in Canada. With one exception, this park had more visitors than any other in this country last year and the year before. We found that previous years of neglect, money voted and not spent, had to be met in 1957 with a vigorous and massive development program which resulted in a tremendous expansion in the use of the park by people from all over North America.
I would say to the same minister that the roads to resources program has meant a great deal to our people and has translated, in a few short years what was at one time the province's poor highway system into one of the most splendid highway networks in the dominion of Canada.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) were here I would say that the ARDA program has struck a most generous and appreciative response in Prince Edward Island. Our provincial government, headed by that truly great Canadian the Hon. Walter Shaw, had already embarked upon a program along similar lines which dovetailed magnificently with this program which is known as ARDA. I hope the present Minister of Agriculture or the other one who comes from the east- I suppose we will come under his jurisdiction-will foster and further the development of this magnificent program which is doing so much for the agricultural people of Canada.
I do not know to whom the next item should be directed-perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). If she were here, I would say that we expect the payment of $75 per month to all our people over 65 years of age. This will be appreciated, as was the increase of $19 which was made by the previous government. The increase would only be $10, but we will appreciate it. I was impressed the other day as I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He seemed to be somewhat critical of the Liberal party because, in his view, they had taken a long time to fulfil their promise in respect of hospitalization. I suppose one might say that it was our party that fulfilled that promise for them. However, I would not quibble. The year 1919, to which he referred, happens to be the year of my birth, and therefore I cannot say it is a long time ago.
I am also not prepared to say it is a long time when I recall another promise which was made at another Liberal convention in


the year 1893. This is a most impressive commitment to the people of Canada and was given by the Liberals then assembled. It was that:
-the present constitution of the Senate is inconsistent with federal principles in our system of government and is in other respects defective, as it makes the Senate independent of the people and uncontrolled by the public opinion of the country, and should be so amended as to bring it into harmony with the principles of popular government.
This was a plank in the platform in 1893, in 1896, and I need not ask Mr. Speaker, about the implementation of that plank in an ancient platform. Compared with that, the non-implementation of the hospitalization plank of 1919 may be interpreted as a mere lapse of memory. If there are changes in the Senate, I suspect they will be similar to the changes which have been made throughout the years when the Liberal party was in power.
I would not want to give the impression to the members of the new government that we do not wish them well, that we are not here to assist in any way we can in their policies for the people. I should like, at this time, to compliment the Prime Minister upon having selected one of my Prince Edward Island colleagues for a cabinet post. I will not make any comparisons on the importance of the post formerly held by my colleague, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) and the post of Solicitor General. I will only say that I am delighted that the Liberal party, after a quarter of a century, has honoured one of the members from Prince Edward Island by giving him a cabinet position. I extend to the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) my good wishes as he takes on his duties. I pledge him such co-operation as I can give in the furtherance of the interests of Prince Edward Island.
I should like to say, too, that I feel similarly about the new member for Kings (Mr. Mul-lally). Naturally, I cannot compliment him upon defeating my former colleague, Mrs. MacDonald. However, I wish him well and I will say to him, through you sir, that as always I stand for province before party. If the new government, during its tenure of office can do as well or half as well for Prince Edward Island and for the maritimes in general as its predecessor, they will exceed my expectations, but they will please me tremendously.
There is nothing more for me to do at this stage, but I hope in future days I may have an opportunity to participate in debate. While I may not have been active in some ways, Mr. Speaker, I think no hon. member who has ever come to the House of Commons has moved about as much as I have. I began by sitting on the Speaker's remote right and

now I am on the Speaker's immediate left. Who knows where I will end. In the parliaments of Europe they used to interpret and correlate a position in the chamber with one's political views. To date I have been an extreme rightist and an extreme leftist. Possibly my position merely indicates my party whip wanted to get me as far away as possible, or perhaps it was just an accident of seating arrangements.
We will have a big event in Prince Edward Island in 1964, the place where Canada was born and which is the cradle of confederation. At this early stage I would like to extend an invitation to all hon. members to join with the thousands and thousands of others who are coming to our shores to celebrate that inaugural event. I think we will give you a real eye opener and a worthy prelude to the national celebrations which will take place in 1967.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, I have enjoyed listening to the last remarks of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), particularly with regard to closure. I find them a little surprising coming from one who is a supporter of the right hon. gentleman opposite, the former prime minister, who undertook to do away with closure and then immediately imposed his own form of closure by governing the country, or trying to govern the country, by refusing to allow parliament to discuss a budget for two years and by imposing taxation and surcharges by order in council, again without allowing parliament the opportunity of discussing them.
I should like to congratulate you, sir, on your election as chairman of committees and Deputy Speaker, and I ask you to convey to the hon. member for Mount Royal my congratulations on his election as Speaker, which I add to the many already offered him. I am sure Mr. Speaker's conduct in his high office will be such that it will lend to the increasing demand that his appointment be permanent.
I also want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on his election as Prime Minister, and his cabinet colleagues on their appointments. I am sure the trust that millions of Canadians have placed in him will be fully justified. I further want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the creditable manner in which they performed their task, which has brought honour and distinction to their respective ridings.
I would like to thank the people of my own riding, particularly those who voted for me and worked so hard on my behalf, for
The Address-Mr. Basford giving to me the opportunity, at a fairly early age, of serving in this house and working with other hon. members in making this country a better place for all of us. I would also like to thank my fellow Liberal party members from British Columbia in doing me the honour of selecting me as chairman of the British Columbia caucus.
I think I speak on behalf of all new members on both sides of the house in thanking those hon. members re-elected in the last election for the very warm and gracious way in which they have welcomed us to the house, and for the very helpful way in which they have endeavoured to get us going on our parliamentary duties.
I have not had the opportunity of talking with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), but I am sure when I do his welcome will be tinged with a certain regret because, Mr. Speaker, I have the honour- or at least I regard it as an honour-of belonging to a very select group on this side of the house who defeated New Democratic party members of parliament in the recent election. The N.D.P. group in the house has grown smaller as a result of the April 8 election, and I predict that in the years and the elections to come they will grow smaller still.
If the government is allowed by hon. gentlemen opposite to get on with the job of governing Canada and carrying out its program, of which the speech from the throne is only a first instalment, we will be able to show that this party and this government are the really effective element of reform in Canada, and that the New Democratic party, by fighting or refighting the class wars of 50 years ago, is becoming increasingly old fashioned and out of touch with Canada's twentieth century problems. In passing, I would say to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), because I know the N.D.P. well, that I think the Sergeant-at-Arms should be left where he is rather than put in the centre of the aisle.
It is traditional in maiden speeches to describe in some detail the beauties of one's own riding. I -would like to describe the beauties of my riding and of the west coast of Canada, but the beauties of the west coast are so great that they are indescribable. Rather than describe them I would like to invite all hon. members to come out to the west coast of Canada to see the sort of very beautiful country we have there.
To hon. members who do not know my riding I point out that it is purely urban, situated in the central part of Vancouver and having both residential and industrial sections. While I hope to speak from time to time in the

The Address-Mr. Basford house with regard to problems of special concern to my riding, such as waterfront development, False Creek harbour development and the Kitsilano air force station which is located in it, at the present I just want to mention it is a purely urban and downtown riding.
Because it is situated right in the city of Vancouver, the general prosperity and welfare of the people of my riding, like that of all people in Vancouver, are dependant largely upon the success of Vancouver becoming the major trading port that it can become. At the present time to handle the people and commodities arriving at our international airport and through our harbour, 24 consulates, five trade commissioners, 21 customs house brokers, 15 shipping agents, 47 shipping company representatives and 26 freight forwarders now make Vancouver their operational base. Because of the importance of trade to Vancouver, and because of the importance of Vancouver becoming the trading centre that it can and must become, I welcome the references in the speech from the throne to the fact that the government will pursue an active and expansionist policy with regard to trade. The welfare of Vancouver and the west coast generally depends on Canada having the freest possible degree of trade. In this particular connection I would like to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister and his colleagues the application of the city of Vancouver for a centennial Pacific trade centre. I shall quote briefly from the application of the city of Vancouver with regard to this trade centre:
There is reason to expect Canada's exports to northeast and southeast Asia, Australasia and the west coast of the Americas will flow through British Columbia ports at the rate of more than $2 billion a year a decade from now.
To secure this trebled increase and to improve upon it, and in so doing help correct Canada's urgent imbalance in world trade, requires bold, new-fashioned formulas to withstand competition from the aggressive new Europe and the United States.
The Pacific centennial trade centre is proposed as one such bold, new-fashioned formula.
It is the contention of the city of Vancouver that the centennial Pacific trade centre, bringing together under a common roof all traders with Pacific interests, not only will meet the foreseeable demand but, more, will be the prime agent creating it.
It seeks the impetus of the senior government.
This is an application by the city for the construction of a huge trading centre in Vancouver. I would urge upon the Prime Minister that at the appropriate time he give this application the attention it deserves so that we may have constructed in Vancouver a monument not so much to what has been done as to what the port of Vancouver can become.


My riding of Vancouver-Burrard is wholly urban. Vancouver, like every major city in Canada, has at its centre areas of blight, decay, ruin and slum. While there are many charming residences in my riding, there are also accommodations in which no human being should be expected to live. I am sure some of the agriculturists opposite would refuse to put some of their animals in such accommodation. For this reason I welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne foreshadowing the establishment of a municipal development and loan board as well as changes in the National Housing Act which, I am sure, will provide cities and municipalities with increased financial assistance in respect of slum clearance and urban redevelopment. I would hope that the mayor and aldermen of my city, as well as those of all other Canadian cities, are farsighted and imaginative enough to take full advantage of this municipal program when it is established.
There are those in our cities who regard slum clearance and urban redevelopment as a luxury which municipal taxpayers can ill afford. On the contrary, slum clearance makes good economic sense. Apart entirely from the social and human values involved-and these should not be minimized-it is of real advantage to municipal taxpayers to redevelop their blighted and slum areas. A decayed area brings little or no revenue to a city, yet the major part of every city's police costs, fire costs, welfare and other costs is spent in these non-revenue producing areas. The largest burden for servicing these blighted and decayed areas falls not on those areas but on the non-slum areas. It therefore makes good economic sense for cities to redevelop these areas and bring them back into active and proper use producing tax revenues for their municipalities.
I had not intended to mention anything about the fishing industry but the subject was raised this afternoon by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson). I wish to say only that I welcome the statement in the speech from the throne with regard to the establishment of a 12-mile territorial limit recognizing the treaty rights and historic rights of others. I am sure that in the atmosphere which now prevails under a government which is dealing with our friends as friends and not as enemies, we shall shortly be able to establish a 12-mile limit and thus give to our fisheries on both coasts the protection they need.
I should like to compliment the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) for having come to British Columbia only a few days after

his appointment and sat down with representatives of our fishing industry, our vessel owners, the union and the native brotherhood to discuss the problems of the industry and to hear the representations, made to him with regard to changes in the international north Pacific fisheries convention. I compliment the hon. gentleman on having taken quick and decisive action in this regard and on saving the NORPAC treaty and the international control of fishing in international waters when it was in great danger of collapse. I disagree with what was said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley and compliment the Minister of Fisheries on his conduct.
I welcome the statement in the speech from the throne that the government will be establishing a commission to study biculturalism. There are those who may wonder why people in British Columbia are concerned about this subject when we are so far removed from the scene of action but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we as Canadians are as concerned as anyone else about the present stresses and strains within our confederation. I hope this royal commission will produce at least some of the answers to the problem. I hope that all Canadians, whether we be English speaking or French speaking, will act with understanding and maturity because, if we do, we can surely provide a system by which the rights and privileges of all Canadians are protected and recognized within confederation.
However, in this discussion of biculturalism let us not forget another group of Canadians, those who have come from afar to make their homes in Canada. I ask the indulgence of the house before reading part of a letter which was delivered to me on election day. I might add that it made the afternoon of election day a little more pleasant.
I am authorized by a few dozen naturalized new Canadians to address myself to you on behalf of all of us.
Having discussed thoroughly the question of voting today, we have decided all to vote for the Liberal party on April 8, 1963.
The motives of our unanimous decision were:
We have full confidence as working people and as members of an ethnic group that the Liberal party government will secure for us more jobs, and that the new Liberal government will have also more understanding for our own, as well as for all Canadian ethnic groups, their cultural, social and political needs and aspirations.
Please convey this our feeling of confidence directly to the hon. Lester B. Pearson with the expression of our highest esteem for him.
I urge the house not to forget in our consideration of biculturalism that there are thousands of people, those of whom the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) spoke so eloquently, who have come to Canada to build new homes and new lives. In some cases the countries from which they came have been
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner destroyed or have disappeared. These people want to play their part, and an important part, in helping to build this country into the great nation which I am sure it can become.

a basic concept which will apply all across Canada, treating all parts of Canada equally alike. ARDA is a very good example of this. The stabilization board is a very good example of this, as is the Farm Credit Corporation and many others which can quickly be cited. I would question very much whether the Department of Agriculture needs two ministers actually to increase efficiency in that department. I would like to point out that this step does nothing for any particular part of Canada but it may do something for a particular political party which has been trying to favour itself at the expense of all Canada over the last five years.
We in western Canada heard a lot about this $2 per bushel of wheat, so perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will bear with me if I come back to it for a moment. I might say that No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 wheat are all supposed to be scaled below $2 a bushel. What of barley and oats? What of Durum wheat? Does there not have to be a relationship between your crops in the acreages allotted? We do not want to have western Canada growing nothing but wheat and no oats or barley. We have seen during the last year or two a shortage of oats in western Canada. A year ago oats had to be imported from the United States. If wheat is priced at $2 a bushel and oats at only 50 cents a bushel, what will the farmer grow? Of course he will grow more wheat than formerly. He will take acres out of oats and put them into wheat, and we will have again to import feed grains into the country, which is likely to occur in years ahead with a Liberal government, and have a surplus of grain.
We in western Canada paid particular note also to the fact that the wheat board and board of grain commissioners were taken out of the Department of Agriculture and placed once again into the Department of Trade and Commerce. Many farmers have asked me why this was done. I am a person of nonpartisan views in many cases. I had a number of Liberals and a tremendous number of N.D.P. people supporting me and voting for me, but the only true answer I could give them was that there was a political reason for the government taking this step. It was taken a day or two after the government took office. I ask, why would a minister from Toronto sell more wheat and feel more responsible to sell wheat than one who had grown up and been raised in the wheat growing areas of western Canada? Mr. Speaker, I should now like to leave the subject of agriculture and deal with another question. Many of my constituents looked to the speech from the throne to find a ray of hope or an assurance that they may have a job tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. I refer in this connection particularly to the operations of the C.N.R. railroad and transportation by rail generally. I read the speech from the throne and found very little reference to rail transportation, railway line abandonment, and so on. I found no guarantee that any significant legislation would be forthcoming in this regard. The other day questions were asked in this house with regard to the discontinuance of railway services from Winnipeg to Calgary. These questions were asked because the people in those areas are concerned about this matter. I refer to the people who are receiving benefits from these services and the people operating the trains. This is just one more step in the operations of the C.N.R. The policy of the C.N.R. is to continually take away services and eventually abandon the line if possible. The policy laid down by the president of the C.N.R. is that the railroad should become bulk haulers and they should do away with all other types of traffic. It is strange to me, Mr. Speaker, that a bus can run along a highway and carry passengers, when its maintenance costs are higher and fuel consumption, and so on, are higher than is the case with many railway lines. On the railway you have smaller inclines and no breaking up of roads which causes wear on tires, or anything of this sort. The question was asked the other day about trains Nos. 9 and 10 being discontinued. There is no regular bus route to replace these trains. No other means of passenger service will be implemented or could be implemented. Since the change of government the railway have failed to take into consideration the needs of this area in what might be called the south central part of the prairies.
We know the railroad operations will come up for review in the sessional committee which will be set up very soon, I hope. This committee will study the yearly operations of the C.N.R. This house knows my feelings with regard to the management of the C.N.R. A fellow by the name of Coyne entered into saving Mr. Gordon's neck a few years ago. In any case, I hope that sessional committee will study the expenditures and operations of the C.N.R. very, very closely. This railroad did away with firemen. They are now trying to lengthen their runs; they are trying to run


through divisional points and lengthen the runs so they may last, particularly in winter, from six to 16 hours. No man can stay on the job day in and day out for 16 hours without its having some effect upon his health or the proper fulfilment of his duties. We have already increased the operational duties of the sectionmen, while at the same time cutting down on the help. To me and my constituents this appears to be nothing more than a matter of increasing the hazards of railway travel. One can only note that the accident rate on the railways has gone up and is going up and this emphasizes the fact that the direction of movement of railway management can only lead to an increase in the accident rate.
I do not want to go into the question of railway deficits. We all know that the C.N.R. took over many uneconomic lines. We all know that in some cases some lines may perhaps have to be abandoned in all parts of Canada. But I do think we all agree that in most cases the C.N.R. has a duty to provide a service and a means of transportation for the goods and commodities produced by the people of Canada.
My constituency along with several others is going to be affected a great deal by any changes in transportation policy that may result from the MacPherson report. I was vitally interested in the legislation proposed by the former government and I looked in the speech from the throne for some assurance of the continuation of jobs in the field of railway transportation. We find little assurance. We will once again watch for any legislative development on the part of the government to provide assurance to railway workers all across Canada that their jobs will be secure and that the trains and trackage will remain as a prominent part of Canada and the movement of Canadian goods.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to add my own congratulations to the many you have already received on the occasion of your appointment to the high office of Speaker of the house. I wish to pay homage also to the Deputy Speaker. I take this opportunity to congratulate the new ministers who have been called to the cabinet and to encourage them in the hard task that awaits them in order to put our economy back on its feet. I feel sorry for them when I think of the problems their predecessors have saddled them with.
I am very proud to represent in this house the beautiful riding of Longueuil. I take this opportunity to thank my electors who had to choose between the former associate minister

of national defence, a Social Crediter, a member of the New Democratic party and myself. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I have nothing but praise for my opponents who put up a clean fight, without personalities. I would like to mention in particular the Hon. Pierre Sevigny, a veteran, a colonel, a very sociable man, who has many friends and who had been the member for Longueuil since 1958.
Mr. Speaker, it gives a newcomer in politics a great thrill to have defeated a minister at the polls even though certain people try to play down that victory by saying that my opponent's resignation from the cabinet before the election definitely contributed to his defeat. Yet, I can see from my seat one of the ministers who resigned before last April 8; he is still in the house and even goes so far as to vote with the government. The riding of Longueuil is comprised of seven municipalities situated alongside the St. Lawrence seaway, on the very location where the world fair will be held.
During the post-war years, my riding which is at the foot of both the Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges, was invaded by an exodus of Montrealers, mostly people who wanted to build themselves a house surrounded by a lawn and garden. There is a wide variety of houses and the price of properties ranges from $5,000 to $150,000. Some municipalities have set up industrial parks that offer many advantages and where industries will be welcome. In fact, we plan to establish an industrial committee that will encourage industries to settle in our area and will show them the benefits that would accrue to them.
I am very much impressed by the speech from the throne which makes known the great decisions the government intends to take, in spite of the fact that the house was convened so quickly after the election.
My first term in the house gives me the great pleasure to witness how tactful, quickwitted and vigorous is the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) and what a great fighter he is.
Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to hear the remarks made by some members of the Social Credit party about the requests directed during the election campaign by the premier of Quebec to the government that was to be elected.
I find their attitude strange, the more so since, during the election campaign, they gave the premier of Quebec-rather coarsely, some people thought-this ultimatum: Mind your own business, otherwise we will fight you in the next provincial election.
The Address-Mr. J. P. Cote
Another thing I have found out in the short time I have been here is that the Union Nationale party has its representatives right here in this house, who repeat the speeches made by the leader of the opposition in Quebec. It would be unfortunate that the interruptions of these hon. members, by their arrogant tone and their partisan spirit, should harm the harmonious discussions that might otherwise take place.
I must also point out, Mr. Speaker, all the admiration I have for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has I believe, all the qualities of a born opposition leader. As this job is very important in an efficient government, I hope, for the welfare of the country, that he stays in his present position for many years to come.
The province of Quebec has elected more members from the Liberal party than from any other party, for it feels confident that the government of Canada, headed by the Liberal party, will be able to uplift the national economy, to curtail the plague of unemployment which is with us at present, by taking appropriate steps to create new jobs, to give to the country a flag and a national anthem, to set up an inquiry on biculturalism and to bring back order in the public service, so as to make it compulsory for certain civil servants or officials of crown corporations to be bilingual, so that bilingual government employees get a higher salary, and that French Canadians can pass tests in their own language, according to their culture and their education.
The province of Quebec has voted Liberal, for it knows that the Liberal party understands its financial problems as well as its claims in this field, and that it will give it its fair share.
In my capacity as chairman of the school board of Longueuil, I can easily understand the financial problems now facing school boards.
To make up for the time lag in the field of education, the Quebec government must take early steps. And these steps, of course, are very expensive. Under the old regime, the salaries of teachers and day labourers were equal, which created a shortage of teachers. But for the last few years, teachers' salaries have doubled in some cases, and we realize now that we are short of normal schools to train potential teachers. It is essential that the Quebec school system be as good as any in the world.

The Address-Mr. J. P. Cote
The people of Quebec have become aware of certain weaknesses in the field of education. But the reforms they have already initiated are very costly and are proving too heavy a burden for the taxpayers. That is why the government of that province claims from the central government its taxation rights as well as authority to establish a national lottery, which seems to me most justified.
Joint programs have not always been favourable to the province of Quebec. A striking example of this is the program for the building of technical and vocational schools. That five year program, which was established in 1957, aimed at giving the provinces 75 per cent of the construction costs of such schools. Well, schools are not built for the sole purpose of taking advantage of a grant; sites had to be chosen and the schools built according to the local needs and in compliance with the new program for technical training.
In 1962, when that joint program came to an end, the province of Quebec was just beginning to carry out the construction of certain technical and vocational schools. When the youth minister asked the federal government to extend the joint program in order that Quebec might be able to take advantage of it, he was informed that the program might be extended for another six months.
How many schools can be built in six months? Can you imagine the millions of dollars the province of Quebec is going to lose because of such a stand? I am convinced that the new government will treat Quebec with fairness in that matter.
Mr. Speaker, the strength of Quebec stems from its financial independence within confederation. When the province has to beg, it loses its pride. The more autonomous Quebec will become, the weaker the separatist tendencies.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that my insistence on that point shall be forgiven; but I am convinced that a just and well-balanced distribution of taxation would unite strongly together, in one confederative state, all our Canadian provinces.
My very presence in this house proves my faith in confederation, but we must all admit that Quebec has an important part to play within confederation, and that is to assert the French fact throughout Canada. And the other provinces should understand that the French language in Canada must not be restricted to the Quebec boundaries, no more than the French Canadians should think that the English language must stop at the Quebec boundaries. When a Canadian from another


province goes to Quebec, he has the right to expect that he may be spoken to in English but when a French Canadian leaves his province, is he not entitled to be answered in his own tongue? It is the same country, Mr. Speaker, and in a bilingual country, must only the French Canadians be bilingual?
In the province of Quebec, there is no problem between the different ethnic groups. You must not think that barricades separate neighbours of different races. A large number of people in Quebec are English speaking; we are proud to have them among us, and I am sure that they are also proud to be from Quebec.
If we can get along wonderfully on the provincial level, why could we not do the same on the federal level? The province of Quebec wants to be acknowledged as an integral part of confederation. French Canadians want to feel at home from Halifax to Vancouver. But to achieve this, we would have to be welcomed in other provinces, and be able to find there advertisements and directions written in French in public places. But alas, outside Quebec, French no longer exists.
I urge Canadians of all racial origins to visit the province of Quebec so that we can show them fine Quebec hospitality and to what extent we are bilingual.
Mr. Speaker, one cannot expect the problem of biculturalism and bilingualism to be settled in a few months, but if all Canadians do their share, it will disappear with time, and all Canadians will benefit from greater understanding and love of each other.

Mr. Speaker, my first words must be words of congratulation to you upon your elevation to your high office. It is a position that I know you will fill with dignity and with fairness to members in all parts of this house. I extend congratulations also to the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Lamoureux) upon his appointment to the post of Deputy Speaker, and to my fellow maritimer in his capacity as deputy chairman of committees. I should like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) for the capable manner in which they discharged their duties in moving and seconding the address. To the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his colleagues in office, I extend congratulations. They have inherited a house and a country left in good order.

This is indicated by a report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald under date of April 19, which reads as follows:
Canada's economy registered an 8 per cent gain last year in the value of its total production. The gross national product, the value of all goods and services produced, rose to $40,401 million from the revised 1961 figure of $37,421 million. In volume terms output rose 6.2 per cent. It was the largest economic advance since 1956.
In April of the past year our foreign reserves of gold in U.S. dollars had risen to $2,671,400,000. A reserve of this magnitude is no mean inheritance for our new finance minister. This situation was brought about by the sound policies adopted by the former Conservative administration.
In the field of trade, Canada had reached an all-time high in 1962. Our merchandise trade surplus amounted to $80 million following upon a surplus of $124 million in 1961. These are the only two years of surplus in the last decade and they reflect the substantial improvement which has taken place in Canada's trade position since 1956 when our merchandise trade deficit was in excess of $700 million. The financial newspapers of this country indicate that in 1962 manufacturing, construction and outlays for new machinery and equipment jumped by 8 per cent. Canadians were producing more, were selling more, were earning more and saving more than ever before in our history.
Now, during the recent election campaign we heard from the present Prime Minister during a visit to Milford, Nova Scotia, that we in the Atlantic provinces have been left far behind in terms of the national economy. He asked for support so that he could get the economy going again and restore confidence. Well, Mr. Speaker, his assertion must have been based on the assumption that the economy had stopped. When you say you want to get something going again, it must have stopped. If the present administration can get the economy going to the extent there is an increase of more than 8 per cent in the gross national product in a single year, all of Canada will be grateful to them and we will not judge them too harshly on their performance with regard to the first 60 days of decision, in office.
The speech from the throne is a fascinating document not only for the policies it contains but also for those which it neglects to mention. When speaking in Milford, the present Prime Minister said, with reference to unemployment, that 250,000 new jobs must be provided in each of the four years a government should last. He said there was also a problem in relation to those unemployed by automation and the Liberal plan called for supplementary retraining benefits to assist the long term unemployed. Where are these
The Address-Mr. Crouse benefits listed in the throne speech? He also called for a revival of the West Indian trade and a policy calculated to make the Atlantic provinces full partners in confederation. In so far as West Indian trade is concerned he said:
-the Liberals wanted to get that going again. This may require special Canadian aid to the West Indies, especially since the current $10 million aid program expires on March 31.
The Conservative administration, Mr. Speaker, provided aid to the West Indies and early in January 1963 the first fruit shipment from Jamaica in 25 years arrived in Halifax for distribution to the maritime provinces. According to the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, this was a shipment of 13,000 cases of citrus fruit valued at $100,000. We are selling to Jamaica seed and table potatoes, Nova Scotia apples, eggs and balsam Christmas trees. However, I see no mention in the throne speech that will further assist in promoting and extending this new trading pattern.
We in Nova Scotia well remember the economic benefits that accrued to our province when trade between the maritimes and the West Indies was flourishing, and we would urge the present administration to carry out its promise, and do everything possible to expand the West Indies trade in keeping with a start already made by the Conservative administration. Our agricultural economies complement one another and industries can be developed in our coastal provinces using Canadian skills and Canadian materials to service the Caribbean market.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister outlined a plan to award 10,000 annual scholarships of $1,000 each to send needy students to university, and on tax sharing he called for the restoration of the principle of equalization payments to ensure poorer provinces would get per capita revenues from personal and corporation taxes equal to the income of the richer ones. What happened to these promises, listed as items we cannot afford not to do? There is no mention of these in the throne speech.
Perhaps these will be done later, along with the other unfilled promises, to provide legislation to establish national marketing boards for farmers, payment of family allowances for children past the age 16 if they remain in school, a special committee to study the problem of railway branch line abandonments, amendments to the federal labour code to provide a $1.25 hourly minimum wage, 40 hour work week, a distinctive national flag, free milk for school children, improved livestock grading, and continued freight assistance for the movement of feed grains to

The Address-Mr. Crouse our eastern farmers. What happened to those promises, Mr. Speaker? They are not listed in the throne speech.
During the election campaign we heard many promises. But the Canadian people have become accustomed to action under the Conservative government and they will expect performance, not platitudes from the Liberal administration.
There is one chapter in the throne speech that has a special appeal to me, and I quote:
It is only with courage and perseverance and hard work that we will achieve the better lile that is within our power, for ourselves and for our children.
Our progress is the work of all the people. In a free country we are all responsible.
This is the basic ideal of the truly free enterprise spirit that made Canada great, and for which my constituency of Queens-Lunenburg is well known. The people of my riding are strongly independent, believing in the capitalistic free enterprise system. Predominantly farmers, lumbermen and fishermen they make their living from primary industries and they must work long hours to provide for their families. A visit to the riding will show the fruits of their efforts, for Queens-Lunenburg is one of the prosperous beauty spots in Nova Scotia.
It is interesting to talk to these people. In their view there has been too much emphasis placed upon the importance of the government, at all levels. As a result governments have grown in size, and the expenditures of all levels of government and the taxation which they necessitate, are at levels which tend to put brakes on our economy. Government featherbedding adds to costs, and increases the inclination to import from other countries, thus contributing to our international balance of payments problem.
In the opinion of my constituents, taxation, especially direct taxation, has the effect of choking off business recovery and stifling expansion. This is understandable when we realize expenditure by our governments represent about 33 per cent of the gross national product of this country. In the United States government expenditures represent about 29 per cent of the gross national product, and Canada today is in the unhappy position of offering less reward for enterprise and initiative than our friendly neighbour to the south. It should be the other way around when we consider some of the handicaps under which we operate.
Competition for the tax dollar between the federal government on the one hand, and the provinces and municipalities on the other, gives rise to more acute difficulties than are found elsewhere. Expenditures of the provinces and municipalities are now estimated

to represent 16 per cent of the gross national product, compared with only 9 per cent ten years ago. The present figure is close to the requirements of the federal government. Provinces and municipalities are constantly under pressure to increase their spending and many proposals are prefaced with the statement "Canada is rich enough to afford these improvements." There is apparently no feeling of responsibility for the national interest, which is regarded as the concern of the federal government. It was this scramble for taxes by the three levels of government which was one of the reasons for the appointment of the Rowell-Sirois commission 26 years ago.
With some provinces now asking for an even greater share of federal revenues, I would urge the government to give careful consideration to our present taxation problem. Some method must be found whereby individuals and corporations can retain a greater share of their earnings for investment in Canadian companies, for it is only through the expansion of our secondary industries under private enterprise that we can overcome some of our unemployment problems.
The government's stated intention to establish a department of industry to work with provincial governments and provide a special thrust for industrial development in areas of chronic unemployment, is a good move. However, I would like to ask the government if this has to be discussed and approved by provincial authorities? There will be some overlapping with provincial departments, but no doubt this can be worked out. However, I believe the taxation problem should first be examined, so that individual Canadians can more fully participate in their country's development.
I note with interest the government's intention to bring in amendments to the Atlantic development board, and its plan to make $100 million available to initiate projects and help lift up the economy of the region. This of course will be welcome news to all those living in the Atlantic provinces, for Canadians generally cannot expect our region to remain economically depressed forever. We deserve equality of opportunity because of our historic past and our contribution to Canada as a nation. However, it is evident the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) had nothing to do with this legislation because in his royal commission on economic prospects, as recorded at page 99 of his report, he stated he did not believe in ad hoc projects and handouts.

It is interesting to note that it took a Conservative government to lead the way in a much more generous manner than the present administration, in keeping with the Atlantic resolutions made by the Conservative candidates at that famous conference in Moncton in the spring of 1957. This boils down to $20 million a year for each of the five years, and the question arises regarding the method to be used for the division of this money.
